Section 3 • Transmitted Flux

3.6 Flux Fluctuations

Up to this point, the discussion has focused on the absorption and transmitted flux along a single sightline, labelled in the straight-line approximation by its transverse comoving position \(\vec{x}_{\perp}\). In many applications, however, one is interested not only in an individual transmitted-flux profile, but also in the statistical fluctuations of that quantity across an ensemble of sightlines or realizations. For that reason, it is convenient to introduce a normalized fluctuation field built from the transmission and its mean value.

Note that the quantity we compute from the gas, \(T = e^{-\tau}\), is the transmission, not the flux. The flux measured by the observer along a given sightline is \(F = F_0\,T\), where \(F_0\) is the unabsorbed continuum of the background source as received by the observer. This continuum is sightline dependent (for quasar spectra it is usually written \(C_q\)), so in this subsection we denote it by \(F_0^{(s)}(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda)\). Following the convention of observational Ly\(\alpha\)-forest analyses, the fluctuation field is defined as the observed flux divided by its expectation, the continuum times the mean transmission. The continuum then cancels, and the fluctuation field depends only on the transmission.

In the remaining of this subsection – for notational purposes, and to avoid crowded expressions – we will simply denote a given line by the index “\(j\)”, dropping the contextual species index “\(i\)”. The fractional flux fluctuation field, or overflux, associated with transition \(j\), for a given realization \(s\), is then defined as \begin{align} \delta_{j}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) &\;=\; \frac{ F_{j}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) }{ F_{0}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right)\bar{T}_{j}\!(\Lambda) } -1 = \frac{ T_{j}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) }{ \bar{T}_{j}\!(\Lambda) } -1, \tag{3.26} \\ \bar{T}_{j}\!(\Lambda) &\coloneqq \left\langle T_{j}^{(s)}\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) \right\rangle_\mathrm{ens} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad T_{j}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) = \bar{T}_{j}\!(\Lambda) \left[ 1+ \delta_{j}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) \right] . \notag \end{align}

Interactive

Here \(\bar{T}_{j}(\Lambda)\) denotes the mean transmission associated with line \(j\) (in the literature usually written \(\bar{F}\) and called the mean transmitted flux fraction). It is a common convention to interpret this quantity as an ensemble average at fixed spectral coordinate (rather than as an average along a single sightline), and is therefore generally regarded as a smooth function of wavelength or, equivalently, of the absorber redshift associated with that wavelength. Consequently, \(\langle \delta_{j}^{(s)} \rangle_\mathrm{ens} = 0\) at every \(\Lambda\), whereas the mean of \(\delta_{j}^{(s)}\) along a single sightline does not vanish in general. Normalizing each sightline by its own mean transmission would define a different field.

If several lines contribute simultaneously, and the set of lines under consideration is \(\{j=1,\dots,L\}\), then the total transmission is: \begin{align} T^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) = \prod_{j=1}^{L} \bar{T}_{j}\!(\Lambda) \left[ 1+ \delta_{j}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) \right]. \tag{3.27} \end{align}

The total mean transmission can be computed as: \begin{align} \bar{T}\!(\Lambda) \coloneqq & \left\langle T^{(s)}\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) \right\rangle_\mathrm{ens} = \left\langle \prod_{j=1}^{L} T_{j}^{(s)}\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) \right\rangle_\mathrm{ens} = \left\langle \prod_{j=1}^{L} \bar{T}_{j}\!(\Lambda) \left[ 1+ \delta_{j}^{(s)}\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) \right] \right\rangle_\mathrm{ens} = \notag \\ & = \prod_{j=1}^{L} \bar{T}_{j}\!(\Lambda) \left\langle \prod_{j=1}^{L} 1+\delta_{j}^{(s)}\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) \right\rangle_\mathrm{ens} , \tag{3.28} \end{align}

and the total overflux is given by \begin{align} \delta^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right)+1 \coloneqq \frac{ F^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) }{ F_{0}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right)\bar{T}\!(\Lambda) } = \frac{ T^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) }{ \bar{T}\!(\Lambda) } \notag = \frac{ \displaystyle \prod_{j=1}^{L} \left[ 1+ \delta_{j}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) \right] }{ \displaystyle \left\langle \prod_{j=1}^{L} \left[ 1+ \delta_{j}^{(s)}\left(\vec{x}_{\perp},\Lambda\right) \right] \right\rangle_\mathrm{ens} }. \end{align}

Remark on the mean flux model.

As previously indicated, generally in Ly\(\alpha\)-forest analyses, the mean transmission is usually modeled as a redshift-dependent quantity, often denoted by \(\bar{F}(z)\). In that sense, the averages introduced above should be understood as ensemble averages at fixed \(\Lambda\). In particular, Eq. (3.28) shows that, in general, \begin{align} \bar{T}\!(\Lambda) \neq \prod_{j=1}^{L}\bar{T}_{j}(\Lambda). \tag{3.29} \end{align}

In a general form and expanding order by order the product in the numerator of Eq. 3.29, we have: \begin{align} &\prod_{j=1}^{L}\left(1+\delta_j^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda)\right) = \underbrace{ 1 } _{\textrm{order 0}} + \underbrace{ \sum_{j=1}^{L}\delta_j^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) }_{\textrm{order 1}} + \underbrace{ \sum_{1\le j_1<j_2\le L}\delta_{j_1}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda)\,\delta_{j_2}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) }_{\textrm{order 2}} + \notag \\ &\quad + \underbrace{ \sum_{1\le j_1<j_2<j_3\le L}\delta_{j_1}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda)\,\delta_{j_2}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda)\,\delta_{j_3}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) }_{\textrm{order 3}} + \cdots + \underbrace{ \prod_{j=1}^{L}\delta_j^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) }_{\textrm{order $L$}} . \tag{3.30} \end{align}

Therefore, for the denominator we obtain: \begin{align} &\left\langle \prod_{j=1}^{L} \left[ 1+ \delta_{j}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) \right] \right\rangle_\mathrm{ens} = \underbrace{ 1 } _{\textrm{order 0}} + \cancelto{0}{ \underbrace{ \left\langle \sum_{j=1}^{L}\delta_j^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) \right\rangle_\mathrm{ens} }_{\textrm{order 1}} } + \notag \\ &\quad + \underbrace{ \left\langle \sum_{1\le j_1<j_2\le L}\delta_{j_1}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda)\,\delta_{j_2}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) \right\rangle_\mathrm{ens} }_{\textrm{order 2}} + \underbrace{ \left\langle \sum_{1\le j_1<j_2<j_3\le L}\delta_{j_1}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda)\,\delta_{j_2}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda)\,\delta_{j_3}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) \right\rangle_\mathrm{ens} }_{\textrm{order 3}} + \notag \\ &\quad + \cdots + \underbrace{ \left\langle \prod_{j=1}^{L}\delta_j^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) \right\rangle_\mathrm{ens} }_{\textrm{order $L$}} = \notag \\ &\quad = \underbrace{ 1 }_{\textrm{order 0}} + \overbrace{ \underbrace{ \sum_{1\le j_1<j_2\le L} C_{j_1 j_2}(\Lambda) }_{\textrm{order 2}} + \underbrace{ \sum_{1\le j_1<j_2<j_3\le L} C_{j_1 j_2 j_3}(\Lambda) }_{\textrm{order 3}} + \cdots + \underbrace{ C_{1 2 \cdots L}(\Lambda) }_{\textrm{order $L$}} }^{\coloneqq \mathcal{C}(\Lambda)} = 1 + \mathcal{C}(\Lambda) , \tag{3.31} \end{align} where \(C_{j_1 \cdots j_n}(\Lambda) \coloneqq \langle \delta_{j_1}^{(s)}\cdots\delta_{j_n}^{(s)} \rangle_\mathrm{ens}\). Note that the order-1 term vanishes only because each \(\delta_j\) is normalized by its ensemble mean transmission, Eq. (3.26).

Substituting Eq. 3.30 and Eq. 3.31 into the total overflux expression, Eq. 3.29, we can write: \begin{align} \delta^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) &= \frac{1}{1 + \mathcal{C}(\Lambda)} \left[ \underbrace{ - \mathcal{C}(\Lambda) }_{\mathcal{S}_0^{(s)}(\Lambda)} + \underbrace{ \sum_{j=1}^{L}\delta_j^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) }_{\mathcal{S}_1^{(s)}(\vec{x}_{\perp},\,\Lambda)} + \underbrace{ \sum_{1\le j_1<j_2\le L}\delta_{j_1}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda)\,\delta_{j_2}^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) }_{\mathcal{S}_2^{(s)}(\vec{x}_{\perp},\,\Lambda)} + \cdots + \underbrace{ \prod_{j=1}^{L}\delta_j^{(s)}(\vec{x}_\perp, \Lambda) }_{\mathcal{S}_L^{(s)}(\vec{x}_{\perp},\,\Lambda)} \right] \notag = \\ &= \frac{1}{1 + \mathcal{C}(\Lambda)}\sum_{p=0}^{L} \mathcal{S}_p^{(s)}(\vec{x}_{\perp},\,\Lambda) \tag{3.32} \end{align}

Where we have defined: \begin{align} &\mathcal{S}_0^{(s)}(\Lambda) \coloneqq -\mathcal{C}(\Lambda), \qquad \mathcal{S}_p^{(s)}(\vec{x}_{\perp},\,\Lambda) \coloneqq \sum_{1\le j_1<\cdots<j_p\le L}\; \prod_{r=1}^{p} \delta_{j_r}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{x}_\perp,\Lambda\right) \quad \textrm{(order $p$)}, \qquad 1\le p\le L, \notag \end{align}
